CARES Project Status

Status date: 2026-11-16
Overall maturity: documentation plus an initial Python prototype; not an operational cybersecurity platform.
Implementation phase: architecture and discovery. No product implementation phase is complete.

Executive summary

The repository is a small Python package with three modules: in-memory asset licensing, a permissive tenant-access predicate, and a local AI policy/status abstraction. Five standard-library unit tests exercise a small subset of those behaviors. There is no API, dashboard, agent, ingestion pipeline, persistent storage, PostgreSQL integration, real AI SaaS client, deployment, or operational security control.

The earlier implementation must be treated as a prototype. Its tests demonstrate selected in-process behavior, not end-to-end product capabilities or security assurance. The architecture documents created alongside this status report describe a proposed design and do not claim that design has been built.

The architecture refinement adds a deterministic identity-claim proposal, PostgreSQL transaction/constraint design for asset quota, AI provider privacy and egress controls, and a measurable initial event-capacity profile. These are documentation-only proposals. Capacity numbers, retention defaults, provider policy, identity confidence rules, and deactivation grace require owner/privacy/legal approval; none have been benchmarked or implemented. Round 1 PostgreSQL logical schema design (entity catalogue, logical ERDs, transaction boundaries, open-decision register, and design changelog) is now documented as a proposed baseline; it is not implemented, not migrated, and not validated by database or security tests.

Review findings on prototype code

PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL is not integrated. No database dependency, connection configuration, SQL, ORM, schema, migration, transaction, row-level security policy, or integration test exists. Current state is in-memory Python dictionaries and lists. The database in the target design is a mandatory future implementation, not an operational service.

External AI

There is no real external AI provider integration. AIProviderConfig stores descriptive values; api_key_env_var is unused. AIProvider.can_process evaluates a classification, and MELIRAAIService.process returns ready, blocked, or unavailable. Even ready does not send a request. No API key is loaded, no HTTP client is used, no provider response is parsed, and no SaaS call has been tested. Therefore MELIRA is not functional.

The current redactor is unsuitable for privacy enforcement: replacing every period is not IP detection; the host= / user= replacements can leave original values after the inserted marker; there is no structured filtering, file-content policy, secret detection, IPv6 handling, or transmission test. The tests do not establish that restricted data is absent from an outbound request because no outbound request exists.

The provider catalog, explicit region/retention/training checks, consent, SSRF protections, secret rotation, usage budgets, and request audit are all proposed Phase 8 work. The requirement for external SaaS and no local inference is mandatory; supported vendor list and customer key-custody model still need owner decisions.

Event capacity and scale

The proposed initial planning envelope is 10 tenants / 5,000 active assets, 25 EPS sustained and 100 EPS for five minutes, 1 KiB average event, and 256 KiB maximum event. The proposed ingest/worker latencies, PostgreSQL reference environment, 30-day event retention, partitioning and expansion thresholds are recorded in DATA_ARCHITECTURE.md and ADR 0005. They are assumptions pending owner approval and benchmark evidence, not current capacity or service commitments.

Asset identity and one-device-one-asset

The narrow implementation deduplicates only when callers submit the same stripped stable_identity value under the same tenant. It does not derive or reconcile stable identities across agent/integration records. Two strings for the same real device consume two slots; one reused string can conflate distinct devices. It does not use IP as its key, which is positive but insufficient to satisfy device identity requirements.

Quota enforcement is a sequential in-process check with no locking or persistence; a race can exceed quota in a concurrent server. The quota is a single constructor value shared across tenants rather than independently configured per tenant. Source IDs are an in-memory set, not durable source objects. Removal pops the asset from the active map, losing accessible lifecycle state; the generated ID based on current map length may be reused after removal. No production billing claim is justified.

The proposed alias namespace, deterministic match rules, pending identity workflow, manual merge/split audit, PostgreSQL locking and uniqueness constraints, lifecycle reservation, and race-condition tests are design work only. The recommended 30-day quota reservation after last-source deactivation is a policy proposal, not confirmed billing behavior.

Tenant isolation

AccessController.can_access compares the User object's tenant to a requested tenant, or allows any user whose caller-supplied role equals administrator. These dataclasses are constructible by any caller in the library; there is no trusted authentication or membership lookup in the decision, no check that the target tenant exists, and the tenant registry is not used by can_access. An administrator has unrestricted cross-tenant access through the helper, with no scope, reason, expiry, or audit. No application or database enforcement exists. The test only checks two outcomes for a manually constructed object. Tenant isolation is not secure or verified.

Test suite

The tests use Python unittest; five cases cover the narrow behavior listed above. They do not test concurrency, restart persistence, database constraints, access-control bypass, event lifecycles, provider network calls, secret handling, privacy-redaction quality, or end-to-end flows. The test suite is not a security certification.

Immediate risks and gates

  1. Do not represent PostgreSQL as available until the application connects, migrations run, and integration tests verify persistence, constraints, and RLS.
  2. Do not represent tenant isolation as secure until authentication, trusted membership, service authorization, RLS, and comprehensive cross-tenant tests exist.
  3. Do not represent MELIRA as functional until an explicitly selected external provider is called in integration tests and policy is proven to gate all transmission.
  4. Do not represent commercial asset counts as correct until canonical identity reconciliation and concurrent per-tenant quota enforcement are durable and tested.
  5. Do not advance to production deployment before threat controls, backup/restore, audit, monitoring, and security testing have evidence.
  6. Do not advertise the proposed capacity figures, retention periods, or provider capabilities as commitments until owners approve and benchmark/contract evidence exists.

Next authorized step

The next step is owner review of the proposed canonical identity rules, pending/quota-reservation semantics, deactivation grace and release policy, event capacity profile/retention, and MELIRA provider/consent/data-processing policy. No further application feature implementation has been started in this task.
